title: Panama Declares 'Major Disaster' After 7.7 Quake as Aftershocks Rattle Country
excerpt: President Mulino says the country faces a “major disaster” as 27 are injured, towns are cut off and more than 80 aftershocks follow Friday's 7.7-magnitude earthquake.
body:
• President José Raúl Mulino declared Panama is facing a “major disaster” after Friday's 7.7-magnitude earthquake, saying some roads had “completely collapsed” and the town of Tonosi in Los Santos province was cut off entirely — reachable only by air.
  • At least 27 people were injured and buildings collapsed in the central provinces of Herrera, Coclé, Veraguas and Los Santos; no deaths had been confirmed as of Friday evening, though authorities cautioned the toll could change as assessments continued.
  • More than 80 aftershocks were recorded, including a 6.6-magnitude quake hours after the main shock and tremors of 5.8 and 5.5. The Pacific tsunami warning issued for nine countries was later lifted.
  • The Panama Canal Authority said canal operations continued normally — a key detail for global shipping — while schools were closed nationwide and Panama City's metro halted service as residents evacuated high-rises.

Panama's president has declared a “major disaster” after Friday's powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake devastated parts of the country's central provinces, collapsing roads, damaging churches and homes, and triggering more than 80 aftershocks that kept frightened residents sleeping outdoors.

“We are facing a major disaster,” President José Raúl Mulino said after the quake, adding that some roads had “completely collapsed.” Health Minister Fernando Boyd said the worst-affected areas were the provinces of Herrera and Coclé, along with Los Santos in the southeast. The town of Tonosi in Los Santos was completely cut off. “We are trying to figure out how to get there by air, because it's impossible by land,” Boyd said.

A day of violent shaking

The main shock struck at 12:56 pm local time on Friday, centred about 12 km west-southwest of Pitaloza Arriba, a remote community in Herrera province, at a shallow depth of around 12 km. The US Geological Survey initially reported the magnitude as 8.0 before revising it to 7.7. Roughly three hours later, a 6.6-magnitude earthquake hit 14 km west of Río Grande, and the local geosciences institute went on to record more than 80 aftershocks — including tremors measuring 5.8, 5.5 and 5.2.

A US tsunami warning covering nine Pacific nations was issued and later lifted after no significant waves materialised. About 4.6 million people experienced moderate to severe shaking, with violent intensity near the epicentre.

Damage and injuries

Images verified by Reuters showed a damaged church and collapsed buildings in Penonomé, a city in central Coclé province. A video showed a bridge over the Panama Canal shaking violently while remaining upright as vehicles crossed. Former president Ricardo Martinelli posted photographs on Instagram of his collapsed house in Sona, Veraguas province. Omar Smith of the National Civil Protection Service said damage was concentrated in the central provinces, with no damage reported in Panama City at the time — though the capital felt prolonged shaking, offices released employees early, traffic snarled, the metro halted service, and schools were let out early nationwide.

“It was horrible, like nothing we ever experienced. My daughter was trapped in school.”

— Juana Alveo, Penonomé resident, to AFP

“We felt it very strongly. It knocked things over in the kitchen, but we're okay, though we're very scared,” Rosendo Domínguez, 60, of Herrera province, told the Associated Press by phone. “Everyone is outside, scared.” At least 27 people were reported injured; no fatalities had been confirmed as of Friday evening.

Diaspora angle

For Indian readers, the reassuring datapoint is the Panama Canal Authority's confirmation that canal operations continued normally — the waterway remains a critical artery for global trade, including India-linked shipping. The quake is a reminder of the region's seismic risk for the small Indian business community in Panama City and for travellers heading to Central America.

What's next

With aftershocks continuing and Tonosi still cut off, the immediate priority is reaching isolated towns and completing damage assessments — a task complicated by collapsed roads. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he was closely monitoring the situation. Whether the injury toll climbs as rescuers reach remote areas will become clear in the coming days.
